parakeet: This reframing has profound psychological consequences. When holiness is equated with separation, in group identity hardens into moral superiority. Those inside the boundary are not just different, they're better. Meanwhile, those outside the boundary are not merely unfamiliar, they're suspicious. Curiosity gives way to caution. Empathy is constrained by fear of contamination. Moral worth becomes something possessed rather than practice. Over time, this produces an us versus them moral lens that feels righteous rather than defensive. People learn to interpret discomfort with difference as discernment and withdrawal as faithfulness. Compassion becomes conditional, extended primarily to those who already belong. The moral imagination narrows because engaging deeply with outsiders threatens the very identity that holiness is set to protect. This holiness model creates boundary obsession. Communities become preoccupied with who is in, who is out, and who is a little too close for comfort. Energy that could be spent addressing harm or fostering care is redirected toward maintaining distinction. Moral exceptionalism takes root. The belief that one group operates by a higher standard simply by virtue of separation. Accountability weakens inside the group while suspicion intensifies toward those outside it. This framework stabilized hierarchy and exclusion.
